newsitem.title: UK: Robust UK retail sales will not tip rate scales.
newsitem.headline: Robust UK retail sales will not tip rate scales.

text.p: A rebound in British retail sales has tempered the evidence of sluggish spending in the run-up to Christmas, but sales were nowhere near strong enough to demand a near-term interest rate rise, economists said on Wednesday.

With the Bank of England apparently toning down demands for higher rates, figures showing sales up by 0.6 percent in January and 4.6 percent higher than a year ago, will not cause Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke any sleepless nights.
But neither do the figures suggest that high street spending is drying up.
"Clarke is home and dry until the election," said Kevin Gardiner, UK economist at Morgan Stanley.
The ruling Conservative Party must hold elections in the next three months and, trailing badly in the polls, will be keen to avoid tighter monetary policy.

In December, economists were shocked by a 0.8 percent fall in retail sales, which called into question concerns about runaway high street spending. But Gardiner said monthly wobbles were nothing new. He noted the three-month rate of sales growth compared with a year earlier was a robust 3.9 percent.

"We, and the Treasury, forecast consumer spending will rise 4.25 percent in 1997. Here is the first snapshot of the year and it is up 4.6 percent on an annual basis," Gardiner said. "Talk of slowing high street spending is massively overdone.
Office for National Statistics figures showed retail sales up 4.6 percent year-on-year last month.

Nonetheless, with Bank of England Governor Eddie George telling politicians on Monday that the need to raise six percent base rates was "less pressing" than he had thought in December, these figures are unlikely to change his mind.
Minutes from January's monetary meeting showed George still strongly recommended a quarter-point rate rise but Gardiner at Morgan Stanley said that was no more than fine-tuning.

"In the last few weeks, the Bank has shown a tendency to want to tinker with rates but you cannot fine tune the UK economy," he said. "You have to hit inflation with a big stick if necessary but the Bank does not seem prepared to do that."

A hefty 1.4 percent rise in textile, clothing and footwear sales in January suggested non-essential consumer spending is still buoyant -- people have money to spend. A solid but unspectacular 0.7 percent increase in household goods sales confirmed that.
The ONS said clothing sales had recovered particularly well since December as have sales of furniture.

"There is fairly robust underlying growth in retail sales still," said Robert Pryor, economist at HSBC James Capel. "The theory that things are beginning to slow down, which in our view has always been exaggerated, may not be right."
Wednesday's public sector debt figures also indicated that consumers are ready to part with their hard-earned cash.

January, a month which saw the government pay nearly six billion pounds of its debt bill, boasted a huge influx of value added tax receipts -- about two billion pounds more than in the same month last year.

"Could that really translate into weak retail sales?," asked Nigel Richardson, head of bond reasearch at Yamaichi International. "I think not." He had forecast a 0.7 percent jump in January sales, well above the consensus for a 0.3 percent rise and much nearer the reality.

But it will take more than Wednesday's figures to maket Kenneth Clarke, who must be increasingly confident of his monetary stance as the Bank of England cools its rhetoric, even consider a pre-election rate rise.

"Today's report does not imply a consumer sector which, at this stage, threatens to undermine and otherwise modestly favourable inflation picture," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at BankAmerica.
